about: Simulator: osmosis and water potential. Model code: bio/assets/tools/bio-tool-math.js (ApBioMath.osmosis). Validator: scripts/lib/apbio-tool-checks/osmosis.mjs recomputes the stimulus table, the numeric answers and the model's behavior (direction of water movement, plasmolysis, lysis).
intro: Put a potato core, a red blood cell or a dialysis bag into a solution. Compare the water potential inside and outside, see which way water moves, and watch the mass change. Run trials across a range of concentrations to build the classic graph, then answer the questions below.
howItWorks:
Water potential ψ = ψs + ψp (in bars). Solute potential ψs = −iCRT, where i is the number of particles each solute unit makes in water (sucrose 1, NaCl 2), C is the molar concentration (mol/L), R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and T is the temperature in kelvins (°C + 273). Pure water in an open beaker has ψ = 0; adding solute makes ψ negative. Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential, and net movement stops when the two are equal.

The model’s assumptions:

  • Water crosses the membrane; the solutes inside the cell or bag and the solute in the beaker do not. Dialysis tubing does let sucrose through slowly: over 30 minutes the effect is small, but over hours the bag’s mass change would shrink.
  • The beaker holds far more solution than the cell, so its concentration does not change. An open beaker has ψp = 0.
  • NaCl splits completely into two ions (i = 2). Real NaCl behaves as about 1.9 particles because some ions pair up.
  • Plant cells (the potato core) have a cell wall. Once the cell is full, the wall pushes back: pressure potential ψp rises as the cell takes in a little more water, which raises its ψ until no more water enters (the cell is turgid). In a strong solution the cell loses water, ψp falls to 0, and the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).
  • Animal cells (red blood cells) have no wall, so ψp stays 0. In a mildly hypotonic solution they swell until the water potentials match; in a strongly hypotonic one (or pure water) they swell until they burst (lyse), here when they reach 1.55 times their normal size (mass and volume change together).
  • Water flows at a rate proportional to the difference in water potential, so changes are fast at first and slow down near equilibrium. Mass change counts only water; part of each cell’s mass (proteins, starch, walls) does not change.
  • The numbers are illustrative: real potatoes differ with variety and storage. Each run adds random scatter (standard deviation 0.8 percentage points), like measurement error.

states.plasmolyzed: Plasmolyzed: membrane pulled away from the wall

systems.name: Potato core (plant cells with walls)

time.hint: Potato cores take hours to settle: 1440 minutes is 24 hours.

systems.note: Potato cells start slightly turgid, with cell sap at about 0.33 osmol/L. About 45% of a core’s mass (starch, walls) is not free water.

systems.name: Red blood cell (animal cell, no wall)

time.hint: Red blood cells settle within seconds.

systems.note: A red blood cell’s cytoplasm is about 0.30 osmol/L. It has no wall, so nothing stops it swelling.

systems.name: Dialysis bag (sucrose solution inside)

time.hint: The classic lab weighs the bags after 30 minutes.

systems.note: The bag is loosely filled: it can swell by 30% before the tubing is stretched tight. Set the sucrose inside with its own slider.

osm-s1.title: Potato cores in sucrose solutions
osm-s1.text: Students placed potato cores in sucrose solutions at 22 °C and weighed them before and after 24 hours. The table shows the mean percent change in mass (model data from this simulator).

tables.caption: Mean percent change in mass after 24 hours

questions.q: Using the table, estimate the sucrose concentration at which the cores would neither gain nor lose mass.

why.correct: The mass change crosses zero between 0.2 M (+5.7%) and 0.4 M (−9.6%). Reading across with a straight line gives 0.2 + 0.2 × 5.7 / 15.3 ≈ 0.27 M; the model’s curve crosses at about 0.30 M. Any answer from 0.24 to 0.34 M is a fair reading.

questions.q: Assume the cores neither gain nor lose mass in 0.30 M sucrose at 22 °C. Calculate the water potential of the potato tissue (R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K)).

why.correct: With no net water movement, the tissue’s ψ equals the solution’s. The solution is in an open beaker (ψp = 0), so ψ = ψs = −iCRT = −(1)(0.30 mol/L)(0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))(22 + 273 = 295 K) = −7.35 bar.

questions.q: The cores in 0.0 M sucrose gained 18.4% of their mass, but the cores in 1.0 M lost 36.9%. Which explanation best accounts for the gain being smaller than the loss?
options: As water enters, the wall pushes back and pressure potential rises, so the cells’ water potential reaches zero and intake stops
Sucrose entered the cores in 1.0 M solution, so they lost more mass than water alone could explain
Membranes pump water out of cells faster than water can flow back in, so losses are always larger
No osmosis happens in 0.0 M solution because there is no solute in it, so the cores gain mass only by soaking

why.correct: A plant cell wall limits how far the cell can swell. Turgor pressure (ψp) rises as water enters and raises the cell’s ψ to that of pure water (0), so the gain stops early. In a strong solution nothing limits the loss: water leaves until the cell’s ψs falls to the solution’s, and the cells plasmolyze. (The starting gradient is also smaller in water, about 7 bar against about 17 bar in 1.0 M, but without a wall even that gain would not stop.)
options: Right: rising turgor pressure stops water entry; in a hypertonic solution the cells keep losing water until their solute potential matches the solution’s.
Sucrose entering the cells would add mass, not remove it, and the membrane keeps sucrose out on this time scale.
Water crosses membranes passively, through the lipid bilayer and aquaporins; cells do not pump water itself.
Osmosis is net water movement down a water potential gradient. Pure water has ψ = 0, higher than the cells’ ψ, so water does move in by osmosis.

questions.q: The students repeat the experiment with NaCl solutions instead of sucrose. Assuming NaCl splits completely into ions, at about what NaCl concentration would the cores neither gain nor lose mass?

why.correct: Each NaCl unit makes two particles (i = 2), so a NaCl solution has the same solute potential as a sucrose solution twice as concentrated. The cores balance in about 0.30 M sucrose, so in about 0.30 / 2 = 0.15 M NaCl.
options: This divides by 4: it would match a solute that makes four particles per unit, not NaCl’s two.
Right: with i = 2, half the molarity of sucrose gives the same −iCRT.
This ignores that NaCl dissociates: 0.30 M NaCl acts like 0.60 M sucrose and the cores would lose mass.
This multiplies by i instead of dividing: 0.60 M NaCl has four times the particles needed.

questions.q: Red blood cells placed in distilled water swell and burst, but the potato cells in 0.0 M sucrose do not. Which difference explains this?
options: The potato cells have a cell wall that builds pressure and stops net water entry before the membrane tears
Red blood cells have water channels in their membranes and potato cells have none
The potato cells contain no dissolved solutes, so water does not move into them
The potato cells pump the extra water out with contractile vacuoles as fast as it enters

why.correct: Water enters both kinds of cell in distilled water. The plant cell wall resists expansion, so turgor pressure raises the cell’s water potential until net entry stops. An animal cell has no wall, so its ψp stays near 0, water keeps entering, and the membrane tears (lysis).
options: Right: the wall makes the difference by creating pressure potential.
Both kinds of cell have aquaporins; channels change how fast water crosses, not where it stops.
Potato cells contain plenty of dissolved solutes (that is why the cores gained mass in pure water).
Contractile vacuoles belong to some freshwater protists; plant cells use their wall and turgor pressure instead.

frq.title: Mini free-response question: potato cores
frq.intro: Use the potato core table above (22 °C, 24 hours). R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the potato core experiment.

rubric.point: Independent variable: the sucrose concentration of the solution. Dependent variable: the percent change in mass of the cores. Both are needed for the point.

parts.sample: The independent variable is the concentration of sucrose in the solution (0.0 to 1.0 M). The dependent variable is the percent change in the mass of the potato cores after 24 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the solute potential of the 0.60 M sucrose solution at 22 °C, showing your work. Then use water potential to explain why the cores in this solution lost mass.

rubric.point: Calculates ψs = −(1)(0.60 mol/L)(0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))(295 K) = −14.7 bar (−14.6 to −14.8 bar), with the work shown.
Explains that the solution’s water potential (−14.7 bar) is lower than the tissue’s (about −7.3 bar), so water moves out of the cells, from higher to lower water potential.
accept: the solution is hypertonic to the cells

parts.sample: ψs = −iCRT = −(1)(0.60 mol/L)(0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))(22 + 273 = 295 K) = −14.7 bar. The beaker is open, so the solution’s ψ = −14.7 bar. The potato tissue’s ψ is about −7.3 bar (the cores balance near 0.30 M). Water moves from higher to lower water potential, so water left the cells for the solution and the cores lost mass.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict what would happen to red blood cells placed in distilled water, and explain why potato cells in distilled water do not do the same.

rubric.point: Predicts the red blood cells take in water, swell and burst (lyse), AND explains that the potato cells’ walls build turgor pressure that raises their water potential and stops net water entry, while red blood cells have no wall.

parts.sample: The red blood cells would take in water, swell and burst (lyse), because water enters down the water potential gradient and nothing resists their swelling. Potato cells also take in water, but their cell walls push back, so pressure potential rises until the cells’ water potential matches the water’s and net entry stops.
